subtopic: GUIDE LINES-REQUEST TO REFRAIN FROM ACQUIRING SECURITIES SUBJECT TO U.S. INTEREST EQUALIZATION TAX

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GUIDE LINES-REQUEST TO REFRAIN FROM ACQUIRING SECURITIES SUBJECT TO U.S. INTEREST EQUALIZATION TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the United States balance of payments guide lines were being discussed in this house on February 2, I said that it would be most undesirable if the effect of these guide lines was to induce strong new demands upon capital markets in Canada. I also indicated that if necessary we would take whatever action is appropriate to protect Canadian interests. Prior to our meeting with United States Secretaries in Washington it seemed clear that pressures on our capital markets were being accentuated as an indirect result of the United States guide lines, and we discussed this with them.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
Under the guide lines, United States companies are being encouraged to raise funds abroad for their international operations. In response to this, well known United States companies and their foreign subsidiaries are issuing dollar securities for sale outside the United States. To the extent that this search for funds abroad by United States companies
attracts funds from Canada, it puts abnormal pressure on the Canadian market and could force Canadian borrowers to rely more heavily on the United States capital market.
It has been, and continues to be, the policy of the government to encourage Canadians to invest their savings in Canadian development. We are now entering our sixth consecutive year of significant economic growth. Heavy demands are being made on our capital markets as Canadian industry expands its capacity and improves its efficiency and as Canadian governments and municipalities undertake to provide the many services required by our expanding economy.
To meet this situation I am, on behalf of the government, making the following request today to Canadian investors.
To help ensure that Canadian savings are available to meet the present large demands for capital in Canada the government is asking all Canadian investors, including financial institutions such as the banks, life insurance companies, and trust and loan companies, as well as other corporations, pension funds and individuals, not to acquire securities, denominated in Canadian or United States dollars, which are issued by United States corporations or their non-Canadian subsidiaries and which are subject to the United States interest equalization tax if purchased by United States residents. Investments in such securities made by Canadian financial institutions and pension funds to cover foreign currency liabilities to non-residents of Canada and the United States are exempt from this request.
Canadian borrowers have co-operated with the government's requests in the past for the exercise of some temporary restraint in borrowing abroad in the national interest. I feel certain that Canadian investors on their side will co-operate fully with this request which is also in the national interest.
For some time the Bank of Canada and the Department of Finance have, in answer to inquiries, been discouraging the issue of securities in Canada by foreign borrowers. I feel that we should continue to discourage such issues since the use of Canadian savings in this way could bring increased pressures on our capital market and lead to increased borrowings in the United States by Canadians

March 16, 1966
Finance
under the exemption from the interest equalization tax. I am confident that our financial institutions will continue to assist us in carrying out this policy.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I commend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) for taking this step, but I feel that it is long overdue. I feel that the steps he has taken at this stage are required. I do not know what teeth they may have in them to make sure that these guide lines are followed. I noticed that, according to the minister's statement, investments in such securities made by Canadian financial institutions and pension funds to cover foreign currency liabilities to non-residents of Canada and the United States are exempt from the request. I can understand this provision. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that despite the lateness of this action it does have the effect suggested.

am sure all members will be pleased if the government is taking some measures to protect the Canadian economy against any adverse effects which might arise from the economic guide lines policy of the United States government. I think the minister would have helped the house and the country had he given us some indication of whether or not there has been large scale diversions of Canadian capital either to the United States or to United States investments in other parts of the world. If this has been going on to any considerable extent, I think that we ought to know about it.
We ought to know, second, whether or not the rather bland step mentioned in the statement is a sufficiently strong measure to grapple with the situation. Since we do not know how grave the situation is, we do not know whether the remedy which the minister has proposed is adequate to meet the crisis. I hope that at an early date the minister will tell us how serious is this capital flight. I hope he will also tell the house at an early date whether the measure which he has proposed today is having any beneficial effect. I am sure the house will watch the question with a great deal of interest; and I am also sure we are relieved that the minister is concerned about the matter and is apparently taking at least a preliminary step to cope with the situation.

subtopic: GUIDE LINES-REQUEST TO REFRAIN FROM ACQUIRING SECURITIES SUBJECT TO U.S. INTEREST EQUALIZATION TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the Minister of Finance

(Mr. Sharp) really understands the situation which prevails at this time in Canada in the field of savings and investments.
The Minister of Finance is asking Canadian investors to invest in Canadian industry and borrowers to put an end to their borrowing in the United States.
Well, Mr. Speaker, if you look at the situation squarely, you will note that the biggest borrowers in Canada are the public bodies, namely the federal government, the provincial governments, the municipalities and the school boards.
They are the biggest borrowers and they get most of the savings of Canadians, and today the Minister of Finance is making an appeal to all Canadians, all private investors, in short banks, insurance companies, trust and loan companies, other corporations, pension funds and even private individuals, but he is forgetting the main institution which could solve the problem, namely the Bank of Canada.
The Bank of Canada is a public body which should be responsible for investing in the public sector, that is the federal, provincial and municipal governments and the school boards, thus leaving the private banks free to look after the private sector.
But as long as private savings have to meet the needs of public bodies, governments, I am saying to the minister that there will not be enough private capital in Canada to finance at the same time public and private investments.
Another solution will have to be found instead of the guide lines given at the present time by the Minister of Finance. In my opinion the only solution is to ensure that a public body in Canada, such as the Bank of Canada, can meet the needs of the public bodies, that is the governments. Private enterprise should be left free to meet the needs of private enterprise. Private investors should meet the needs of private borrowers, private companies, and a public body or the Bank of Canada should be given the authority to exist, in order to meet the needs of the public bodies.
That is the only solution and if the Minister of Finance does not want to get that into his head, he will never find another solution to the problems of our modern economy.

Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) for the announcement he has made this afternoon. There were announcements in the press that some large United States corporations were attempting to sell some issues outside of the United States and some rather large figures were involved. Had they moved into the Canadian capital market to raise money for use in their international operations, I am sure it is obvious to all members of the house that things would have been made very difficult for a capital market the size we have in Canada.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
It is not clear, Mr. Speaker, at first glance what the Canadian guide lines will be in the suggestion or the request that the Minister of Finance is making to the banks and to the other sources of credit. However, after we have had a little time to study these several paragraphs in his statement, perhaps it will be more clear.
We join with the Minister of Finance in that part of his statement where he suggests that governments and municipalities are undertaking now to provide for expanded services required in our expanding economy. It is interesting to note that the requirements for these purposes in Canada and borrowings in the United States have gone up from $15 million for the first two months of 1965 to $172,880,000 for the first two months of 1966, which is proof that there is a greatly expanded demand by our municipal governments for funds in this year.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we should like to say very briefly to the Minister of Finance again that this is good and sufficient reason for his taking action that we expand the municipal development fund, and even take some action to set up a municipal development bank, because there is ample evidence now that this is required in Canada. We should not like to see our municipal governments, our school districts and so on being short of funds or having interest rates forced up. We should like to see this expansion I talk of taking place in the country.

subtopic: GREAT LAKES-DISCUSSIONS WITH U.S. RESPECTING ANTI-POLLUTION MEASURES

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Luc Pepin (Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys):
speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
subtopic: GREAT LAKES-DISCUSSIONS WITH U.S. RESPECTING ANTI-POLLUTION MEASURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 8 I was asked by the hon. member for
Water Resources
Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) to make a statement regarding the discussions held in Washington on March 4 and 5 with respect to the urgent problem of pollution on the Great Lakes and with respect to the effects of a law of the United States Congress authorizing a study of the waters tributary to the Great Lakes. I undertook to make such a statement at an early date.
I may say first that the undersecretary and officials of the Department of the Interior of the United States attended the joint meetings in question and participated in a most constructive way in the discussions which were held on the matters which have been mentioned. In addition, I was invited with my officials to visit the Department of the Interior and took advantage of the opportunity which was thus afforded. Good working relations have existed for some time among the experts and specialists in both countries and relevant information is being exchanged freely, as well as views. During my visit we were able to review in particular a number of points pertaining to communication and liaison.
In the communique issued at the end of the ministerial meeting representatives of both governments recognized the serious implication of the recent interim report of the International Joint Commission on pollution in the two Great Lakes mentioned. In addition both sides confirmed the importance of co-ordinating our studies of this entire problem and supporting the program of investigation and research. Due note was taken of the urgency of curbing inflow to the lakes of certain pollutant materials.
May I say in passing that organizational changes have been undertaken recently in both countries to make sure that the federal governments are enabled to assume a more effective role with respect to matters of water pollution. It was valuable to receive in Washington an explanation of the Water Quality Act of 1965 and of the administrative measures presently taken. Our United States friends were most interested, too, in our proposed Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, with central co-ordinating responsibilities in the field of water pollution.
May I add for the information of hon. members that the advisory board to the International Joint Commission forecasts three phases of study of the pollution in the Great Lakes.
The first phase consists of short term concentrated studies to determine the extent,

March 16, 1966
Water Resources
origin and location of pollution in the waters. The second phase consists of continuing studies of the mechanics of the lakes as they affect pollution distribution and assessment of the changing effects of pollutants, and the effectiveness of remedial measures. The third phase consists of research into more effective means of treatment of wastes, the toxic levels of pollutants under Great Lakes conditions, the cycle of eutrophication-I have a technical definition of that, should hon. members want one-and the disposition of pathogenic bacteria and viruses.
The details of the coming summer's work by Canadian governments have been assembled. Essentially they involve sampling of the eastern end of Lake Ontario and of the St. Lawrence River by the Department of National Health and Welfare; of the bulk of Lake Ontario and of Lake Erie by the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, and inshore sampling of the western end of Lake Ontario and of the margin of Lake Erie by the Ontario Water Resources Commission.
The investments made by mines and technical surveys alone, this year, in this research on pollution in the Great Lakes will be at least $600,000 for operation and $400,000 for beginning construction of the first of three research ships.
With regard to United States public law 89-298, this gives the United States Corps of Army Engineers a moderate sum of money to commence preliminary studies on storage and diversion in water basins supplying the Great Lakes system. Because Canadian interests might conceivably be affected by actions ensuing from such studies, I inquired as to American intentions. It was made clear, that the United States is not contemplating any action which would contravene its agreement with us under the Boundary Waters Act, or affect Canadian interests adversely. In this connection I might read a Canadian dispatch from Washington dated March 7, 1966 which represents an attempt to summarize the present situation. I quote-

speechtext:
We appreciate the minister's having made a statement to us as to the scope of his discussions with representatives of the United States government. I do not want to appear to take an unreasonable attitude but the minister will appreciate that while we fully recognize the need for studies, the situation disclosed in the report of the International Joint Commission makes action imperative.
While therefore we are glad to hear of the plans for making studies of water samples from the lakes, we reserve our judgment on the question of whether sufficient action is to be taken. There are three programs of sampling. But here again, though we recognize that studies must be made, it seems that to date we have been given only a forecast of action rather than action itself. This is an urgent problem. I trust, therefore, that the planning and thinking in connection with matter covered in this report are being carried on with a greater sense of urgency than the report itself makes evident.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
The only matter of detail upon which I would like to comment is that I am surprised to find there are apparently to be two agencies of the federal government carrying out sampling for the same basic objective, one the Department of National Health and
March 16, 1966	COMMONS
Welfare and the other the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. I had understood the whole purpose now was to co-ordinate these activities under one agency and I am surprised, therefore, when we start our first study that we are undertaking to carry it out by two different departments.
I am at a loss to understand why that should be so. I think there would be less efficiency and greater cost involved; but I shall reserve final comment until we receive more particulars, and similarly with respect to the matter of the views of the United States officials and their difference of opinion with Mr. Kierans. I hope the minister's estimates will be brought in early in the supply program this year so that we can have the kind of discussion that is essential about this whole urgent matter.

subtopic: GREAT LAKES-DISCUSSIONS WITH U.S. RESPECTING ANTI-POLLUTION MEASURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was interested in the latter part of the observations of the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton). Like him, I was somewhat puzzled by the fact that two federal agencies of government were being authorized to undertake these studies. However, it is possible that these studies may lie in different fields and, on the basis of further information we may be able to get, we can assess whether this is the most economical approach.
On the broader question of the announcement made by the Minister, I am sure all hon. members of the house welcome this indication that some specific action is being taken.
Certainly the reports we have been getting about the increasing level of pollution in the Great Lakes system show that some sort of crash program is required. Whether the study which is being proposed will be expedited to the point where it can launch corrective measures quickly enough to combat the growing level of pollution is questionable, but I think I can best sum this matter up by saying I am glad to see some attempt is being made to lock the door of the barn before all the horses have been stolen.

Mr. Speaker, without detracting from the urgency and importance of the statement the minister has made, we in this group will reserve our observations until we are able to study his report made this afternoon. But I would say it emphasizes in this one area the great importance of an over-all water resources policy which will include the subject of water pollution.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEVELOPMENT OF COMMERCIAL FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in January
of 1964, slightly over two years ago, I had the honour of convening in Ottawa a federal-provincial conference on fisheries development. The outcome of that conference was that the representatives of the federal government and the ten provinces agreed to co-operate in the formulation and implementation of a national development program. Such a program, it was decided, would include measures to expand available resources, measures to improve the technique of catching and processing and to facilitate their adoption, measures to diversify products and improve quality, measures to expand markets and reduce price uncertainty-in short, measures to bring about greater productivity and efficiency in all phases of the fishing industry.
We of the federal government, together with those responsible for fisheries in the provinces, have now had two years in which to formulate and implement, in part, a program to carry out the stated aims of the conference. It need hardly be said that the development and expansion of the fishing industry are rooted in productive capacity at the primary level. To harvest the resources of the seas around us and all our fresh water areas it is necessary that our fishing force, which is large and industrious, be well equipped for its trade. It must also be well trained in both the old methods of operation and in the newer ones which have been introduced in the past few years, and others now being explored.
March 16, 1966	COMMONS
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
To enable the fishing force to obtain the more modern, mechanized equipment-the vessels and gear-that they need, a number of forms of financial assistance already in existence have had to be improved upon and others have had to be inaugurated.
Much has been done in the past two years on development projects and much more is planned with a view not only to the further utilization of the traditional fisheries but also the exploitation of species of fish which are not now taken by Canadian ships. On the Pacific coast, we are encouraging the utilization of the offshore groundfish resource and exploring ways and means of making use of such species as dogfish to provide a new source of income for fishermen. We foresee also a very substantial development in the herring fishery, particularly in the Atlantic, where our fishing fleets, inshore, near offshore and deep sea, are undergoing the expansion and modernization which is imperative if we are to meet the increasing market demand for our fish products.
A new fishery is shaping up in the form of a substantial tuna development which is being established in New Brunswick. This in itself is unique in that it inaugurates what we might call the first far distant fishing operations by Canadians.
I could list scores of projects which are under way or planned for fisheries development. Some of these are being carried out by my department at 100 per cent federal cost, while others are joint endeavours in co-operation with the provinces and the industry.
I must emphasize that our total fisheries development program will stand or fall on the availability of qualified fishing crews both in the inshore and offshore fisheries. This very real manpower problem is presenting a major challenge to the provincial as well as the federal authorities. However, we are determined to meet it head on and to this end there is close federal-provincial co-operation not only in the design of vessels and improved fishing methods generally but in what we hope will be effective vocational training activities.
Development of the resource itself is fundamental to any development or expansion of the fisheries. I am gratified and impressed with the total response of our resources development personnel in all parts of Canada to the intricate demands which confront them in this regard. I say "intricate" demands for it is in this field that we attempt to improve upon
DEBATES	2781
Commercial Fisheries Development the natural environment of the fish and try to reduce or eliminate the damages caused by industrial and other uses of water resources. I shall have much more to say in this regard, Mr. Chairman, when the estimates of the Department of Fisheries are discussed before the Standing Committee on Fisheries.
The addition of industrial and other wastes to fresh water contribute to massive changes in plant and animal life up to and including the fishes. These changes are not really understood and, I am pleased to say, the Fisheries Research Board of Canada is to carry out a program in the area to identify what these changes are and why they occur.
This particular program is just one of many which will be launched by both Canada and the United States under reference to the International Joint Commission.
In keeping with the vigorous industrial and resource development programs there has been simultaneous and effective expansion of the technological and biological programs of the Fisheries Research Board of Canada. In other words, development of the fisheries and broadening of scientific research have gone hand in hand as they must.
Today there is virtually no part or aspect of fisheries which does not come under the influence of science. As fishing techniques and methods of processing and of handling fish change, and as we seek to move out into new areas and to develop untapped resources, the active support of science becomes ever more vital. I am impressed that the Fisheries Research Board has found it possible to cope with its increased work load which has taxed its men and facilities to the utmost.
The excellent reputation which our Canadian fish products enjoy on the domestic market and in the many countries to which they go is indicative, I think, of the efforts of our industry to diversify their products and to maintain high standards of quality. It reflects also, I think, the contributions in the inspection field which my department has made in promoting high standards.
A major advance was accomplished with the passing of fresh and frozen fish plant registration legislation which became effective April 1, 1965. Excellent co-operation has been received from industry in meeting the requirements for construction, equipment and the sanitary operation of some 220 fresh and frozen fish processing plants.
The products of our fisheries generally are now enjoying excellent markets; the demand
March 18, 1966

Commercial Fisheries Development is good both at home and abroad and prices are strong. The problem now is one of supply rather than demand, and it is to assure the supply that this Fisheries Development Act, which I now expect to have the privilege to introduce, has been prepared.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEVELOPMENT OF COMMERCIAL FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I listened with interest to the comments of the Minister of Fisheries, as he announced the details of a measure for the development of the commercial fisheries of Canada. This will certainly be a measure that is of considerable importance to Canada and to the Atlantic provinces in particualr.
Since I was first elected as a member of parliament in 1957 I have not been able to avoid feeling that in some parts of Canada the fishing industry is looked upon as being of little or no importance. Fish was something tolerated in the central and western Canadian provinces and on Friday, known as fish day, there was much rejoicing if an alternative to fish could be found. As a result of this attitude the consumption of fish in Canada is still only approximately 13 pounds per person, which is regretable in view of the high nutritional value of high quality sea food.
I welcome the minister's statement and I point out to him that the commercial fishing industry is vitally important not only to the economy of the Atlantic provinces but to Canada as a whole. Last year this industry reached a new peak of production. Nearly
925.900.000	pounds of fish were landed by Maritime fishermen, at a landed value of more than $65 million. When one realizes that marketed values are approximately twice the landed values, it then becomes apparent just how important these dollars are to the Maritime area and to the economy of Canada as a whole.
One cannot help but be impressed by the progress which has been made by the industry in recent years and by the growth of the larger long-liners, draggers and trawlers, which can only be described as bringing about a complete transformation of the industry. Unavoidably this has brought many new problems requiring solutions. A shortage of skilled manpower, as mentioned by the minister, for new ships is already developing. The training of new recruits and of adult fishermen is a problem in itself. In fact, in my opinion the future of the fishing industry in Canada will be jeopardized unless some
10.000	men are trained and added to the 
industry within the next ten years in addition to those who are now engaged in the industry.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
The minister has stated he is aware of this problem but I should like him to be more definite when he outlines the government's program to assist in the training of these men. If we can develop the same progressive approach to manpower policies as we are now developing with regard to the design and construction of ships for the fishing industry, we can be assured of a bright future for this industry. I think the time has arrived for upgrading the industry. The fishermen of Canada's east coast have never had a status in society commensurate with the risks they undertake, the labour they perform and the contribution they make to the economic life of the nation. The income of a fisherman has never been a true reflection of, or a realistic reward for, the risks he undertakes in his profession. However, things are changing, and this measure would indicate that the importance of the fisherman as a producer is being realized not only by the industry but by all levels of government.
I would point out to the minister that the proper management of larger plants and larger fleets of ships is becoming a major problem. The present expanded industry has inherited the facilities of the much older inshore and salt fish industries and there are many communities which have not yet been able to achieve the transformation and equip themselves with the plants, harbours and wharves that a modern, highly competitive industry and trade require. There is a great opportunity in this area for the Minister of Fisheries, in co-operation with the Minister of Public Works, to provide extensive dredging, new wharves and breakwaters which are urgently required and are an integral part of a growing and expanding fishing industry.
Nearly three-quarters of the earth's surface is covered by water. It is the last great frontier on earth. In view of the foreseeable needs of humanity it is not a moment too soon to begin a serious and systematic study and exploration of the potential of the sea.
Our North America fishing industry is still somewhat primitive from a technological point of view. For example, the Soviet Union has increased its fishing production within the past year by 25 per cent. To put Canadian fishermen in their rightful place in world fisheries we must apply advanced technology to the industry without delay. We must tell
March 16, 1966

our problems to the scientists and enlist their aid in solving them. We must search the world for new markets. How many people are aware, for example, of the staggering tonnage of fish which is caught and then shoved overboard because in our western society the catch is considered unmarketable? Surely the industry, the scientist and the technologist can work together to utilize these species for the benefit of humanity as well as providing profit to the industry. Methods of fishing, types of boats and gear not yet used in the Atlantic provinces are proving to be successful elsewhere. There are resources of fish that the Atlantic provinces have not yet tried to exploit, products for which a good price may be obtained; yet no effort has been made so far to produce and sell them.
We must carry out greater studies of the ocean floor along our entire continental shelf. We must study the effect of ocean currents on our fish population. We must study the possibility of developing fish farms especially for the rearing of lobsters, to help improve our inshore stocks which are rapidly being depleted. I suggest that a special "sea grant" be made to our colleges. Such a grant would help to further the studies of those interested in marine science and technology and lead to the increased knowledge by which man will one day, it is hoped, begin to tap more of the untold riches of the sea.
I welcome the measure which the minister has introduced. He has told us his department has adopted improved methods of inspection in the fisheries plants throughout Canada. I commend him for this move because I am sure it is of vital importance that strict enforcement be carried out. It is perhaps one result of slack enforcement in former years that fish were exported or sold in Canada in a condition which only served to blacken the name of a product so vitally important to the economy of Nova Scotia and the Atlantic provinces generally.
I cannot impress on the minister too strongly the need for maintaining strict fisheries inspection. It is essential to the entire industry. We welcome this move. I reserve the right to make further comments when the bill is before us at a later stage.

The fishermen must be aware of these new systems and must understand their operation. They must have a knowledge of the equipment with which they are working. I am sure that in this field alone the government can help in co-operation with the provinces and do much to alleviate the situation existing at the present time. speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should give consideration to the advisability of amending the Canadian Citizenship Act and the regulations made thereunder to provide that (a) an applicant whose application for citizenship is refused be provided with full particulars of the reasons for such refusal (b) a Citizenship Review Board or similar body be established to which an applicant whose application for citizenship has been refused may appeal such refusal (c) Courts of Citizenship be established in more centres across Canada than is now the case (d) Courts of Citizenship should be open during evenings and on Saturdays and, generally (e) landed immigrants should receive much more encouragement and assistance in preparing themselves to become citizens at the earliest possible date after they become qualified therefor.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
He said: I cannot describe to you, Mr. Speaker, the relief one feels on rising to speak on a subject which is, I am sure, entirely non-partisan and which concerns every member of the house. There may be differences of opinion on details as to the best manner in which to accomplish a common objective but I am certain the objective is common to all of us.
May I suggest, first of all, that I am one who is perhaps particularly suited to raise the question of citizenship. I happen myself
Citizenship Act
to be a naturalized Canadian, having been naturalized by my late father back in 1929 as a youngster, and I happen to have gone through in my boyhood after I was 12 the experience of learning a new language and adjusting myself to a new country and a new environment. Accordingly, I have some appreciation of what is involved.
This subject was drawn to my attention particularly during the election campaigns of 1962, 1963 and 1965 in my own constituency and in other constituencies. I have the pleasure to represent a constituency in which there is a very large number of new Canadians, most of them of Italian origin. I found that more than half of these new Canadians who were eligible to be Canadian citizens had not become Canadian citizens. When we started a campaign, I looked at the situation in the riding and was certain there would be many thousands of new Canadians on the voters list. But when the list appeared there were fewer than half the number that might have been expected. When I went around the constituency, having learned a few words of Italian to converse with these people, I found that many of them were frightened about applying for Canadian citizenship because of the qualifications which appeared to be demanded of them before thay can attain citizenship status. It was brought home to me then that we ought to take another look at the requirements as we express them and at the machinery we have provided for those wishing to obtain citizenship.
I say this not because I think any one of us in any corner of this house would have been wiser had we drawn up the original regulations but because I think we should profit by the experience which has now been gained. I wish to make it clear that I do not want to relax the solemnity with which the taking of citizenship should be surrounded. I do not want to relax any of the symbols which should be used to convey to a person about to take citizenship the seriousness and value of this act. I have had the experience, as have other members, of travelling to other countries, in Europe many years ago and more recently in Central and Latin America. During these visits I had an opportunity to see how very highly a Canadian passport is regarded and valued in foreign lands. I say this not in any jingoistic spirit but in a sense of, I hope, pardonable pride. Frequently while walking through the streets of foreign

March 16, 1966
Citizenship Act
countries, or at their customs barriers or immigration gates, the fact that one has a Canadian passport proves to be of great value, and the men or women you meet on such occasions show great respect for it.
For this reason it is important to surround the attainment of citizenship with all the sensible and reasonable solemnity which is necessary to make it a fact of importance to the psychology of the person concerned. But this does not mean we should have provisions in our laws which frighten people. I draw attention, first, to subsections (e) and (f) of section 10(1) of the Canadian Citizenship Act where we say that a person can become a citizen only if he has an adequate knowledge of either the English or French language. Well, Mr. Speaker, I know a great many people born in this country whose mother tongue is one or the other of those languages, yet whether or not they have an adequate knowledge of it depends on one's definition of "adequate". I have met a good many new Canadians and asked them why they had not applied for citizenship. They have replied: Look at the words in the act calling for an adequate knowledge of English or French; you can listen to me, talking in broken English; I obviously do not have an adequate knowledge of English, so why apply to become a citizen?
A provision of this sort does not make sense in a Canadian Citizenship Act. It is the wording which frightens the average person. We must remember that many people who come from other parts of the world may not have had an opportunity of attending school and may not have come here with any great literacy even in their mother tongue. For this reason they may not be equipped to acquire a new language in a way which would satisfy any interpretation of the term "adequate knowledge". But do not misunderstand me. I am not saying that the courts generally impose too strict a definition, though I do think that in many instances the courts have not been very wise about it either and have demanded, in my part of the country, a greater knowledge than is really necessary or sensible. But the words themselves frighten new Canadians; they think they have to know more than, in fact, they need to know.
In my years in Canada since September, 1921, I have known hundreds of excellent Canadian citizens who have lived here for many years with only a very limited knowledge of either of the two Canadian languages. 
This does not necessarily make them less useful or less devoted citizens of this country.
Then we have another requirement which frightens these people. The Act provides that in order to become citizens they must have an adequate knowledge of the responsibilities and privileges of Canadian citizenship and intend to comply with the oath of allegiance set forth in the second schedule. I do not know how many people have an adequate knowledge of the responsibilities and privileges of Canadian citizenship, or indeed, exactly what that term means. I often wonder whether the 20 or 25 per cent of Canadian citizens who do not go to vote on election day are accepting all their responsibilities as Canadian citizens. Yet they are already citizens, either natural born or naturalized. We do not need such statements as these in the Act.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
Let me indicate to the house this simple proposition: that even if a person is not a citizen, if he resides in Canada and is permitted to work here and carry on business here and undertake obligations, responsibilities and liabilities under the laws of Canada to which he is subject, that person is a Canadian in every sense except the important sense of being a citizen, having the right to vote, having the right to carry the Canadian insignia in the form of a passport or whatever document he carries with him when he goes to another country, and having the right to the protection of Canada and the Canadian authorities when he is in a foreign land. We ought to make becoming a citizen easier rather than harder, and I draw a distinction between the solemn act of becoming a citizen and the requirements for becoming a citizen.
Unless I am very much mistaken, my late father became a citizen in 1929 by merely filing an application in the required form, going through a few minor formalities and obtaining a certificate. All of his generation, all of the very large number of people who came to Canada after the first world war and who have made such a tremendous contribution to this country, were not required, as I recall the law and I hope I am not mistaken, to have the knowledge as the language in the act unnecessarily describes it.
My next point, Mr. Speaker, is that at the present time the regulations require an effort on the part of the applicant for citizenship which again, perhaps not entirely reasonably,
March 16, 1966



prevents him from becoming a citizen. Normally he has to take three days off work. He has to appear at the place where he gets the application form. He signs it there. He has to swear an affidavit, and he is expected to appear in person which means one day away from work.
As I read the regulations they require him to appear in person. I think it is subsection 5 of regulation No. 5 which states that a person who resides 50 miles away from the nearest court can make out his application in triplicate and forward it by mail but if he lives within the court area he is expected to appear, make out the application and swear the affidavit. He is then required to appear in court at the hearing of his application. That is a second day away from work. Then he has to appear as a rule in the same court to be sworn in, to take his oath of allegiance, before he can obtain his certificate. That is a third day away from work.
Without exaggeration, Mr. Speaker, I met dozens of men in my constituency during the election campaign whom I asked, "Why have you not applied for your citizenship when you have lived here eight, ten or twelve years?" The answer I received was usually, "Yes, I make up my mind to go and become a citizen but on the appointed day I cannot get there. My work does not let me go and I cannot afford to lose the money."
If a man earns as little as $1.50 or $2 an hour on a construction job which may not be unionized, he will lose 10 hours pay that day, some $15 to $20, and that is why he does not become a citizen. There is no reason why that should be so. There is no reason in the world why Citizenship Courts should not be open evenings or Saturdays or even Sundays. Surely there is no more solemn act, religious act if you like, than the act of swearing allegiance to a new country, and there is nothing incompatible between doing that on the Sabbath and doing any other thing that is holy on a Sunday. There is no reason why we should present difficulties of this sort to the new Canadian who desires to become a citizen. He should not have to take three days off work in order to go through the procedures that are required.

I quite agree, Mr. Speaker. I do not think that three appearances are necessary. The reason I did not suggest that two of them be done away with, although I would like to see them made more voluntary, is that I think if the new Canadian does appear to make out his application in an office specially set aside for that purpose and has a few words with the registrar or whoever may be in attendance, he can receive some explanation of the form he is filling out, something which may be strange to him. That is a useful introduction to the citizenship idea. I do not object to bringing him in and making him feel a part of the machinery, of the procedure, but I do object to having him come in at times which are onerous and costly to him. Certainly there should be a mandatory appearance when he swears the oath of allegiance and becomes a citizen.
I am sure the people in the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, who have had much more experience than I can claim, will be able to think of a dozen other ways by which the procedure and the machinery can be improved. I merely plead with the minister and all those concerned with this aspect of the work that they take a very serious look at present procedures for citizenship, and in particular a look at the language in order to make it less onerous sounding to the new Canadian who wants to become a citizen.
I have had an applicant for citizenship come back to me and say, "I did not make it. You know why? They asked me what was the capital of British Columbia and I said Vancouver. Then they told me it was not, it was Victoria." I will bet you, Mr. Speaker, if I may use this expression with respect, dollars to doughnuts that if you ask people outside this building on Wellington Street here in Ottawa, as you buttonhole them walking along the street, nine out of ten would say Vancouver.

subtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENTS FOR BENEFIT OF APPLICANTS
speechtext: Good for them.

Well, Mr. Speaker, there is one member of the house who is apparently father to the thought and who himself would say Vancouver out of rivalry. The people on Wellington Street may not know any better but that does not make them any the less good Canadians. I would be surprised if some members of this house did not on occasion forget the precise names of some capitals that are close to them. Yet there are people who

speechtext: What is the capital of New Brunswick?

subtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENTS FOR BENEFIT OF APPLICANTS
speechtext:
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) asks what is the capital of New Brunswick. Again I am sure dozens of people passing along Wellington Street would indicate Moncton or Saint John rather than what I hope it is, Fredericton. This kind of thing is unnecessary, Mr. Speaker. There is no reason why people who want to become citizens should know that Fredericton rather than Moncton and Victoria rather than Vancouver are the capitals of the respective provinces.
In our entire general education structure we pay far too much attention to irrelevant fact than to relevant principle. More important for the new Canadian is that he be given a sense of the principle of citizenship, of his duty to the community, of his heart and soul as a Canadian, rather than that he know the name of some capital of the English word for some word in his native language which can have very little relevance to his being a decent, good and valuable citizen.
In the remaining few minutes at my disposal I want to speak on the second part of my resolution, which deals with the fact that too many people are refused citizenship without being given a reason and without having recourse of appeal from such refusal. I have here in my own file three other such cases, which one of my colleagues was good enough to let me study, dealing with people who were refused citizenship during the last few years and had to go through all sorts of convolutions in order to find out what was wrong, what was the basis on which their applications were refused.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
Therefore I suggest we ought to take a look at our statute to see whether or not we can provide at least more particulars, if not full particulars, in respect of any refusal of an application for citizenship, and above all that there be a citizenship review board or a similar body established to which a person who has had his application refused may come by way of appeal. When I am told of cases in respect of which the refusal of citizenship is based on security reasons, which I am sure occasionally is the case, then my answer is, Mr. Speaker, that there have 
been errors on that score as well and that the review body is needed in such cases just as well as in any other case. The procedure of the review body in a case of security may be different and perhaps the hearing might have to be in private but in such cases, as well as in others, it is needed.

speechtext: In your suggestion concerning appeal and in your motion are you suggesting that if such an appeal board were set up-and I agree with many if not all of the things the hon. member states-the board's authority would be absolute once they made their ultimate determination or are you still going to reserve the final stamp of approval for the executive or the government?

speechtext:
I would think the latter. I am not a great expert or even an expert at all in this field. However, I would think the granting of citizenship in cases where there may be some doubt should be the responsibility of the executive in the final stage, although if the minister acted contrary to the finding of the review board he would have to give a pretty good explanation for so doing. If it is thought that the review board should have more authority than this, I have no objection.
I do not have any strong feeling on that score.
I conclude, Mr. Speaker, by saying that I place this resolution on the order paper and spoke today not merely to have a resolution to speak to but because it is a fact that literally tens of thousands of new Canadians in Canada today, as I speak to this house, are eligible to become citizens so far as their residence in Canada is concerned but are not citizens for no other reason than that the present law and procedures either frighten them or make it difficult for them to obtain their citizenship. I think it is unjust to invite people to come to our country and then place obstacles on the road to their becoming citizens. We ought to vest the obtaining of citizenship with all the solemnity, all the respect and all the aura of importance that we can symbolically put together, but we ought to remove every vestige of the kind of thing which places unnecessary obstacles in the way to citizenship for those who have joined our country.

subtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENTS FOR BENEFIT OF APPLICANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the member for Welland, a very cosmopolitan riding, I know something personally of this problem and I know how important it is. Generally speaking I am in favour of the motion. The essence of the motion is that we should encourage immigrants to become citizens and not only should we encourage them to become citizens but that we should improve the procedures. However, this observation should be qualified by the statement that since the inception of the Canadian Citizenship Act in 1947 the machinery for obtaining citizenship by and large has been adequate and on most occasions very fair.
There are many strong reasons why people wish to become citizens. They want to be able to vote, they want to be able to participate in government, they want to be able to feel they are a part of the community and part of the country. However, at the same time there are many factors working against their desire to become citizens. Most of these people come from countries where they have seen much governmental control. They are afraid of signing forms, they are afraid of judges and they are afraid of anything pertaining to courts. The language barrier itself militates against many people applying to become citizens. To counteract these forces I believe that not only the government but also every citizen has a role to play.
I should like to go on record as stating also that our government has not been completely lax in respect of preparing people to apply for citizenship. We do have citizenship seminars. We have lectures provided in most urban and rural centres. There are lectures on history, geography and on the responsibility of citizenship. We have booklets on citizenship. I grant that these perhaps could be improved. However, I should like it to be mentioned that we do have facilities to encourage people to become citizens.
I have mentioned that the government, of course, should encourage immigrants to become citizens, but I think we as Canadians ourselves have a great responsibility. These people are shy and timid and we should in most cases encourage them. We should make
Citizenship Act
them feel welcome. We should help to dispel their fear of courts and procedures. This is our duty as good citizens also.
The suggestion with regard to the need for more courts, of course, is a laudable one. There is, however, always the question of cost and time. I think what is even more important is not the number of courts but the location of the courts. I can cite a very concrete example. At the present time we have a centralized system of Citizenship Courts. We have one in Hamilton, with a branch office in St. Catharines. In my riding we have the cities of Welland, Port Colborne, Niagara Falls and the town of Thorold. These are very cosmopolitan urban areas. There are many people who are seeking citizenship. At one time we had a Citizenship Court in Welland but it was moved to St. Catharines. I know as a matter of record that many possible applicants will not travel to St. Catharines in order to become citizens. This may seem peculiar, but people who are wavering between making a decision and not making a decision make the decision not to go. Therefore I would suggest that a Citizenship Court be re-established in the city of Welland.
One of the prerequisites of obtaining citizenship is an adequate knowledge of the English language, and I think this is right and proper. It is a matter of degree. I do believe that hardship is worked upon older people who would like to become citizens. Again from personal knowledge I know there are many older people of 55, 70 or 75 who would like to become citizens but cannot do so because of the language barrier. I think this is one area in which we certainly should do some revision and provide some remedy.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
In respect of the actual hearing of these cases it has been my experience that by and large the ceremony is impressive and although the procedure is perhaps strict in some cases it is fair and proper. The Citizenship Court judges are on the whole experienced people. They realize how to handle witnesses and on the whole the procedure is carried on with efficiency and dignity. In regard to the submission that reasons for dismissal of an application should be given, I would contend that this is not a practical suggestion. This is not a court of law in which there are litigants and where reasons for judgment are given. This is an application for citizenship and the basic reason for people being denied citizenship is a lack of

Citizenship Act
adequate knowledge of the English language. In that case the application is adjourned and the person tries to improve his knowledge of the language and comes back at a later date.

Not according to my information. As I have stated before, I think the application of the language barrier is perhaps a major weakness. I believe that generally speaking our Citizenship Courts and procedures are fair and just. Naturally any regulation and procedure can be improved upon. I think one of the major areas for improvement in this respect is the location of the courts. In addition, as I stated previously, the question of language should be re-examined and the rule made less stringent.
In conclusion I should like to emphasize that the government has a responsibility to facilitate citizenship applications but we as Canadian citizens have an even greater responsibility. If we wish to smooth the way for these people to become citizens of this country, it behooves all of us as Canadian citizens, regardless of political persuasion, to welcome our new Canadians, befriend them, encourage them and make them feel that becoming a Canadian citizen is worth while.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, could I ask the hon. member a question? Does the hon. member agree with me that we might well consider the automatic granting of citizenship to people who have resided in Canada for five years as long as their record is clean and they have demonstrated good citizenship in those five years?

subtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENTS FOR BENEFIT OF APPLICANTS
speechtext: No, offhand I cannot say that I do. The reason is simply that I think any person who wishes to become a Canadian citizen should go through a certain formal procedure. It should not be so stringent and narrow that to become a Canadian citizen is made difficult but it should be important and impressive enough to make the person feel that citizenship is worth obtaining.

subtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENTS FOR BENEFIT OF APPLICANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words at this time to indicate agreement with the general proposition that procedures for citizenship applications should be eased. I should like to begin by quoting from the conclusion of the Sedgwick report on immigration which came into our hands just yesterday. While this report deals with immigration rather

than citizenship, I think this conclusion applies. At page 20 the report says:
I think the Act should state clearly that admission to Canada, either as an immigrant or non-immigrant, is a privilege and is not to be construed as a right.
I adopt those words in connection with the question of citizenship. Citizenship in this country is a privilege and not a right. At the same time I think that those who would become citizens should not have unnecessary blocks placed in the way. The two hon. members who preceded me mentioned in particular the Citizenship Courts in urban areas. There is another problem that concerns those in rural areas. It is the fact that we do not have Citizenship Courts which are easily accessible to the person who wants to become a citizen.
In the rural areas one has to go to the county or district court office and there apply for citizenship papers. Then one must appear at the formal sessions of the county or district court, be examined by the judge and then be formally admitted as a Canadian citizen. I think this also is an impressive procedure. But there is one shortcoming in this respect, the infrequency of sittings of county and district courts. In Ontario particularly, of which I have knowledge, most of the county and district courts sit only twice a year. If one happens to miss the proper time it may be more than a year before an application for citizenship can be heard, whereas in the Citizenship Court in urban areas applications can come on very quickly.
I should like to mention one matter here that I think is not too well known. Applicants in rural areas have an alternative. They can apply to the County Court and go through the usual procedure or they can go to the nearest Citizenship Court and there take advantage of the fairly quick procedure that is adopted. I think many people delay making application because they are afraid it will take too long and they will become lost in the legal red tape.
I believe that while ease of access to the Citizenship Courts and the formal courts should be maintained, we should never forget the fact that citizenship is a privilege. I think we should make sure that the citizen is received with some formality and has a feeling that he has become, through some official act, a citizen of this country. While the proposition the hon. member put forward today would help, I think we need to give these people a feeling of acceptance and of
March 16. 1S66

the solemnity of the occasion, which is most important.
The question of language has been raised and this also is a problem in many rural areas. I believe that in the areas outside metropolitan centres in which many languages are spoken, it is more difficult for an immigrant to become a citizen. The standard of language is much higher in a rural area where either English or French is spoken mainly and other languages are not used. I believe that particularly in the case of elderly people who come to this country late in life it is difficult, and the language requirement for such people ought to be eased.
I feel that people wishing to become citizens of this country must have a basic knowledge of either English or French. They must have sufficient knowledge to enable them to speak, be well understood and understand what is being said to them. I believe this is essential. But older people in my opinion should be given a break. I think it is more important in many of these cases that the people have a sense of belonging, of being part of Canada, than it is to make provisions with which it is difficult for them to comply.
I wish to make just one more point in closing, Mr. Speaker. In the rural areas I think more assistance ought to be offered to people desirous of becoming citizens. In the urban areas there are Citizenship Courts. The staffs of these courts are there and there are people of the immigrant's own language and ethnic background to help him. These people are able to help because they have been through the procedure before. They know where to go, what to do, what the questions are likely to be and what the answers are.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
It is different in the rural areas because many of those who make applications come from isolated areas. They do not have the assistance and the friendship of people that those who live in urban sections have. I feel that such people require assistance from the government and also require assistance from their member of parliament. I believe this is one duty to which we should pay more attention. Most people who come to this country seem to believe that a member of parliament is a person to whom they cannot have easy access or a person who is not sufficiently interested in them. I think they would find most members of parliament are extremely interested in them, especially when it comes to their first vote. Of course, it is a
Citizenship Act
fact that when they do become citizens they are entitled to vote.
I urge all members of the house to make a special effort to give assistance. I think one of our problems is that in many cases we do not know who is applying. There have been occasions on which Citizenship Courts or county and district courts have helped by giving members lists of people who are about to apply. This is most helpful. I think this is all I want to say. I do agree that the procedures ought to be improved and I approve in principle of the resolution that has been presented.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, am almost in complete agreement with the notice of motion of the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) except as concerns the provision stipulating that
An applicant whose application for citizenship is refused be provided with the full particulars of the reasons for such refusal-
I think there are many reasons to refuse an application and the government should have the privilege of withholding its reasons. Obviously, I do not have the time to elaborate on this point. If I recall what my hon. friend said a while ago, to the effect that admission of an immigrant to this country remains a privilege, I believe that, in all cases, the government should not be required to give to the applicant, at his request, full particulars or reasons for such refusal. Reasons may be given by the government, but to require that they be given could, to my mind, be dangerous.
I have listened to the hon. member for York South who seeks to facilitate the entry of immigrants into the country. If he means to facilitate the naturalization of immigrants who have been staying in this country for a number of years, I am in agreement with him. On the other hand, I think we should make entry of immigrants into Canada more difficult.
I should like to mention instances which have occurred in my province, not to bring up those in other provinces, even though I may leave myself open to suspicion, and I accuse my own province. In Quebec, over the last few years, it has been noted that most troublemakers, who have caused regrettable events reported in the press, were immigrants.

March 16. 1966
Citizenship Act
If the officials of the immigration office had conducted a more thorough investigation into their cases, they might have discovered they were already agitators in their countries. Not so long ago, a lady of virtue, who was refused entry into the United States, was accepted in Canada. It is hard to take: The Americans are harder to please than we are. I think we should make it more difficult to enter the country in order to get the best people, and I am referring to their moral value.
Of course, I am not ruling out the possibility of security in some cases which could eliminate even outstanding people. Once again, I am against making it too easy to enter into the country. I would agree with some of my colleagues who claimed that immigration offices are not well organized. Judging by the situation in my city, there is only one officer in charge in our immigration office. He is away from the office most of the time. Immigrants and businessmen who could hire some immigrants are unable to reach him. There should be at least a staff of three persons in that office. If it is the same throughout the country, I feel the government is not organized as it should be to deal with our immigrants.
In my opinion, the soundest argument of my colleagues-I accept all the rest of the notice of motion-is that they advocate extending the services provided to immigrants after they reach the country. They should be given language courses, in French or in English, a bare minimum, in short, a small stock of 50 or 60 words to enable them to shift for themselves. They should be given lessons in citizenship, so that they might know what living conditions to expect. Why could those offices not be open for a few hours on Sunday afternoon, so that the immigrants might not waste any time? For, though Sunday is the Lord's Day, the ceremony which solemnizes the granting of a Canadian citizenship certificate is closely related to the religious services held on that day.
These are measures which could be adopted so that the immigrants might feel at home, and feel that type of warmth they lacked back home.
But I maintain that it would be unwise to lower the standards for entry to this country. On the contrary, I feel they should be a little more stringent so that we might be sure of welcoming only the best.

Similarly, I would not want to create difficulties for the government by forcing it to reveal all the reasons which might justify refusal of entry, for I feel that if the rest of the motion were applied-there would be representations made to the court, in an endless process, that would cause considerable embarrassment.
Therefore, I support the motion of the hon. member for York South, except for those details.
